name: Nicodemus
role: Pharisee who came to Jesus by night
summary: A Pharisee and a leader of the Jews who came to Jesus at night and was told he must be born again. Later he objected in the council that the Law does not condemn a man unheard, and with Joseph of Arimathea he buried Jesus with about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes.
body: Only John mentions him, three times. He comes by night, acknowledging Jesus as a teacher come from God, and is told that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again. His puzzled questions (“How can a man be born when he is old?”) draw out the conversation of John 3.
When the chief priests and Pharisees want Jesus arrested, he asks, “Does our law convict a man without first hearing from him?” and is mocked for it.
After the crucifixion he brings a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds, and with Joseph of Arimathea wraps Jesus' body in linen with the spices.

later.text: The Gospel of Nicodemus, also called the Acts of Pilate, is a later apocryphal account of the trial and of Christ's descent to the dead, written in his name.

sources.title: Gospel of Nicodemus (Acts of Pilate)
sources.note: dated variously from the 4th century; some material may be earlier

later.text: The Talmud names a wealthy Nakdimon ben Gurion in Jerusalem before its fall. John Gill finds it probable that he is this Nicodemus, since he lived in this age; Heinrich Meyer holds the identity possible but uncertain.
traditions: probably the same man: John Gill

sources.title: Exposition of the Entire Bible, on John 3:1
sources.author: John Gill
sources.note: 'there are some things which make it probable, that he was the same with this Nicodemus; for the Nicodemon the Jews speak so much of, lived in this age'

sources.title: Critical and Exegetical Hand-Book to the Gospel of John
sources.author: H. A. W. Meyer
sources.note: on 3:1: 'The identity of the two is possible, but uncertain.'
